latin: Corruptis omnibus indiuiduis specie humanae haec est uera: homo est animal.
translation: With all individuals of the human species destroyed, this is true: man is an animal.
translation_note: Farmer's note reports that Biondi's Italian translation of the thesis reads 'corruptis' as an accomplished fact rather than a hypothesis, which Farmer says destroys Pico's sense (farmer1998:11003).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch1, from Latin at farmer1998:10929

sources.text: Aristotle, Metaphysics 7.14-15 (critique of the Platonic theory of ideas)
sources.pico_relation: Farmer traces the scholastic background of this thesis to this Aristotelian discussion

doctrine: The thesis states that even if every individual member of the human species were destroyed, it would remain true that man is an animal (farmer1998:10929). Farmer's note reads this as a standard scholastic formula affirming the independence of species and genera from their individual members, traced to Aristotle's attack on the Platonic theory of ideas in Metaphysics 7.14-15 (farmer1998:11003). The same note reports that Pico held species and genera could legitimately be viewed as independently existing from the limited standpoint of human knowledge, though from a higher perspective they are mere beings of reason (farmer1998:11003).
historiography: Edelheit's chapter on Pico and Albert introduces the thesis under the heading 'Thesis 2', framing it as a question about the relation between particulars and universals (edelheit2022:9058). Edelheit's accompanying note reproduces the Latin from the printed edition of the 900 Theses (edelheit2022:9086).
not_established: Context and reception beyond Edelheit's brief gloss are not established by the sources consulted.
